p.src: Now the three disciples went into the hall and said to their master, “The meal is nearly ready. What did you call us for?” Tripitaka said, “Disciples, this is not about the meal. This temple has something called a Ginseng Fruit, shaped like a child. Which of you stole and ate one?” Bajie said, “I am an honest fellow. I know nothing about it and have never seen one.” Qingfeng said, “He is the one who was laughing! He is the one!” Wukong shouted, “This is the face old Sun was born with. Just because some fruit of yours has gone missing, am I not even allowed to smile?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, calm your anger. We are men who have left the world. We must neither lie nor eat food that leaves our consciences uneasy. If you truly ate their fruit, apologize to them and be done with it. Why deny it so stubbornly?” Seeing that his master spoke reasonably, Wukong confessed the truth: “Master, it was not my doing. Bajie overheard the two Daoist boys next door talking about eating some Ginseng Fruit. He wanted to taste one, so he had old Sun knock down three, and we brothers ate one apiece. Now that we have eaten them, what would you have us do?” Mingyue said, “Four of ours were stolen, yet this monk still claims he is no thief!” Bajie cried, “Amitabha! If four were stolen, why were only three brought out for us to share? Someone had already kept one for himself!” The fool perversely began raising a clamor.

p.src: Once the two immortal boys had learned the truth, they reviled them all the more fiercely. The Great Sage was so enraged that his steel-hard teeth ground audibly and his fiery eyes opened wide. Again and again he gripped his gold-banded cudgel, and again and again he restrained himself, thinking, “If the boys merely abuse me to my face, so be it. I will endure their insults. But I will give them a plan that ends the line forever, so that none of them will ever eat the fruit again.” Brave Wukong plucked a hair from the back of his head, breathed an immortal breath over it, and cried, “Change!” It changed into a false Wukong who stayed beside the Tang Monk with Wuneng and Wujing, enduring the Daoist boys’ abuse. His true body sent forth its spirit, mounted a cloud, leaped into the air, and went straight to the Ginseng Fruit garden. Drawing his gold-banded cudgel, he struck the tree with a mighty clang, then exerted his divine strength to push mountains and shift ridges, and toppled the tree with a single shove. Alas! The leaves fell, the branches split, and the roots rose from the earth; the Daoists’ Grass-Returned Cinnabar was cut off forever. After toppling the tree, the Great Sage searched its branches for fruit, but could not find so much as half of one. For this treasure falls when it meets metal. Both ends of his cudgel were sheathed in gold, and iron too belongs among the five metals, so the blow had shaken every fruit down; and once fallen, they entered the earth on touching soil. Thus not a single fruit remained above ground. He said, “Good, good, good! Now everyone’s feast is over.” He put away his iron cudgel and returned directly to the hall. With a shake, he reclaimed the hair into his body. Those mortals of fleshly eyes could not perceive what had happened.

p.src: After the immortal boys had abused them for a long while, Qingfeng said, “Mingyue, these monks can certainly endure an insult. We have scolded them like chickens for all this time, yet not one of them has answered back. Perhaps they truly did not steal the fruit. Perhaps the tree is so tall and its leaves so dense that we miscounted. We must not accuse them unjustly. Let us go and check again.” Mingyue said, “That makes sense.” The two returned to the garden, only to see the tree toppled and its branches split, with every fruit gone and every leaf fallen. Qingfeng was so terrified that his legs gave way and he tumbled head over heels; Mingyue’s waist went limp and he fell sprawling. Both were frightened out of their wits. A poem bears witness to this. p.src: The two lay in the dust, their speech incoherent, crying only, “What are we to do? What are we to do? The source of the elixir in our Five Villages Abbey is ruined, and the lineage of our immortal house is cut off. When Master returns, how can the two of us answer him?” Mingyue said, “Senior Brother, stop shouting. Let us straighten our robes and caps, and take care not to alarm those monks. No one else could have done this. It must have been that hairy-faced, thunder-gobbed rogue. He sent forth his spirit and worked his magic to destroy our treasure. If we confront him, the rogue is certain to deny it, and we shall inevitably quarrel with him; and once the quarrel begins, it will come to blows. How could the two of us possibly defeat all four of them? We had better deceive them. We shall say that none of the fruit is missing, that we counted wrongly, and then apologize to them. Their meal is ready. When they sit down to eat, we will serve them a few extra side dishes. Once each of them is holding a bowl, you stand to the left of the door and I to the right. We shall slam the door shut, fasten the lock, and lock every one of these successive gates, so that they cannot escape. When Master returns, he may deal with them however he pleases. The monk is also an old acquaintance of Master’s. If Master spares him, it will be a favor granted on his account; if he does not, we shall at least have captured the thieves, and may thereby escape blame ourselves.” Hearing this, Qingfeng said, “A good plan, a good plan.”

p.src: The two forced themselves to recover their spirits and put on cheerful faces. Coming directly from the rear garden into the hall, they bowed to the Tang Monk with hands clasped behind their backs and said, “Master, our words just now were coarse and offensive. Please forgive us, please forgive us.” Tripitaka asked, “What do you mean?” Qingfeng said, “None of the fruit is missing. The leaves were so high and dense that we could not see clearly. We went to check again just now, and the number is unchanged.” Bajie seized the opportunity to put on airs: “You ignorant young boys came here hurling wild abuse, cursing us without cause and falsely accusing us. What shameful conduct!” Wukong understood perfectly but said nothing. Privately he thought, “That is a lie, a lie. The fruit is utterly done for, so why do they speak like this? They must have some means of bringing the dead back to life.” Tripitaka said, “Since that is so, bring the meal in. We shall eat and then be on our way.”

p.src: Bajie went to serve the rice, while Friar Sand set out the table and chairs. The two boys hurriedly fetched side dishes—pickled cucumbers, pickled eggplant, wine-lees radish, vinegared bean pods, salted lettuce, and blanched mustard greens—setting out seven or eight plates in all for master and disciples to eat with their rice; they also brought a pot of fine tea and two teacups, and waited attentively beside them. Just as the master and his three disciples picked up their bowls, the two boys, one on either side, slammed the doors shut and secured them with a double-pronged brass lock. Bajie laughed and said, “You boys have got it wrong. The customs here are strange indeed. Why shut the doors and eat indoors under lock and key?” Mingyue said, “Exactly, exactly. For better or worse, finish your meal before we open the door.” Qingfeng cursed, “You gluttonous, thieving bald rogues! You stole and ate our immortal fruit, already committing the crime of taking produce from another’s garden without leave; and then you toppled our immortal tree and destroyed the immortal root of our Five Villages Abbey. Yet you still dare answer back! If you ever manage to reach the Western Heaven and behold the Buddha’s face, it will only be after turning your back, rocking in a cradle, and being born anew!” Hearing this, Tripitaka put down his rice bowl, and his heart grew as heavy as though a stone lay upon it. The boys locked the outer mountain gate and the second gate as well. Then they returned to the main hall entrance and hurled vicious abuse at them, calling them thieves over and over. They did not stop until the sky was nearly dark, when at last they went to eat. After finishing their meal, they returned to their room.

p.src: The Tang Monk reproached Monkey, saying, “You wretched ape, time and again you bring disaster upon us. You stole and ate his fruit, so you ought to have endured his anger and let him curse you a little. Why did you also push down his tree? If the case were brought to court on these facts, even if your own father were the magistrate, he could not decide in your favor.” Monkey said, “Master, do not make a fuss. Those lads have gone to bed. We need only wait until they are asleep, and then we shall set out tonight.” Sha Monk said, “Brother, every gate has been locked and fastened tight. How are we to leave?” Monkey laughed. “Never mind that, never mind. Old Monkey has a way.” Bajie said, “As though I feared you had no way! With one transformation you can turn into some insect or leech and fly straight out through a lattice hole. It is we who cannot transform who will suffer, left here to take the blame.” The Tang Monk said, “If he should do such a thing and leave without taking you and me, I shall recite that old familiar scripture. How could he bear it then?” Hearing this, Bajie was both worried and amused. “Master, what are you talking about? In Buddhism I have heard of the Śūraṅgama Sutra, the Lotus Sutra, the Peacock Sutra, the Guanyin Sutra, and the Diamond Sutra, but never of any ‘Old Familiar Sutra.’” Monkey said, “Brother, you do not know. This band I wear upon my head was given to my master by the Bodhisattva Guanyin. Master tricked me into putting it on, and it took root as it were, so that I could never hope to remove it. The spell is called the Tight-Fillet Incantation, or the Tight-Fillet Sutra. That is the ‘old familiar scripture’ he means. Whenever he recites it, my head aches; thus he has this means of mastering me. Master, do not recite it. I shall never betray you; I guarantee that we shall all leave together.”

p.src: By the time they had finished speaking, darkness had fallen, and presently the moon rose in the east. Monkey said, “Now all creation is silent and the icy moon shines bright. This is the perfect time to leave.” Bajie said, “Brother, do not play tricks. All the gates are locked. Where can we go?” Monkey said, “Just watch what I can do.” He took the golden-hooped staff in hand, performed an “unlocking spell,” and pointed it at the gates. With a sudden clatter, the paired bolts of gate after gate dropped away, and the doors flew open with a crash. Bajie laughed. “Fine skill! Even a locksmith working his pick could not open them so neatly.” Monkey said, “What is remarkable about these little gates? Even the Southern Gate of Heaven would open if I pointed at it.” They invited their master through the gates and helped him onto the horse. Bajie shouldered the luggage, Sha Monk led the horse, and they headed straight westward. Monkey said, “Go slowly for a while. Let Old Monkey see to it that those two lads sleep for a month.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, you must not harm their lives; otherwise you will add murder for gain to your crimes.” Monkey said, “I understand.” Monkey went back inside and came to the door of the room where the lads slept. He carried sleep insects at his waist, which he had once won from Virūḍhaka, the Heavenly King of Increase, while playing a guessing game at the Eastern Gate of Heaven. He took out two and flicked them through a gap in the window. They flew straight onto the lads’ faces, and the two sank into snoring slumber from which they could not hope to wake. Only then did he stride away upon the clouds, catch up with the Tang Monk, and race straight west along the main road.

p.src: All that night the horse never halted, and they journeyed until dawn. Tripitaka said, “This wretched ape has tormented me to death! Because of your gluttony, you have dragged me through a sleepless night.” Monkey said, “Do not keep complaining. It is daylight now. Rest as best you can in the woods beside the road, recover your strength, and then we shall go on.” The elder had no choice but to dismount and sit beneath a pine, using its roots for a meditation couch; Sha Monk set down the luggage and dozed; Bajie pillowed his head upon a stone and slept. Only Great Sage Sun remained full of spirit: look at him leaping into the trees, swinging from the branches at play. We leave the four pilgrims resting there.

p.src: Now the Great Immortal, after the assembly at the Palace of Primordial Commencement had dispersed, led his young immortals out of Tushita Heaven, descended directly from the jasper sky, and brought his auspicious cloud down before the gate of Wuzhuang Abbey on Longevity Mountain. When he looked, he saw the abbey gates wide open and the ground swept clean. The Great Immortal said, “Qingfeng and Mingyue have made themselves useful after all. Ordinarily, even when the sun is three poles high, they will not straighten their backs; yet today, while we were away, they were willing to rise early, open the gates, and sweep the grounds.” The young immortals were all delighted. But when they reached the main hall, there was no incense burning and not a soul to be seen. Neither Mingyue nor Qingfeng was anywhere about. The immortals said, “Perhaps, knowing we were away, the two of them stole something and fled.” The Great Immortal said, “That is absurd! How could cultivators of immortality harbor such wicked intentions? They must have forgotten to close the gates last night and gone to bed, and this morning they have yet to wake.” The immortals went to the door of their room and found it truly shut, while the two slept inside, snoring deeply; no matter how those outside pounded on the door and shouted, they could not rouse them. The immortals pried open the door, seized the two, and dragged them from the bed, yet still they did not wake. The Great Immortal laughed. “Fine immortal lads you are! One who has attained immortality is so full of spirit that he no longer thinks of sleep. Why, then, are you so drowsy? Could someone have played a trick on them? Quickly, bring some water.” One lad hastily fetched half a cup of water and handed it to the Great Immortal. The Great Immortal recited an incantation, took a mouthful of water, and sprayed it over their faces. At once the spell of sleep was broken.

p.src: Only then did the two awake. They suddenly opened their eyes, rubbed their faces, and looked up to recognize their immortal master, the Lord Equal to the Age, together with their immortal brothers and all the rest. In alarm, Qingfeng bowed his head to the ground, while Mingyue kowtowed and said, “Master! Those monks from the east, whom you called your old friends, are a band of savage and ruthless robbers.” The Great Immortal smiled. “Do not be frightened. Tell me slowly what happened.” Qingfeng said, “Master, not long after you left that day, a Tang Monk from the Eastern Land did indeed arrive. There were four monks in his company, or five travelers counting the horse. Your disciples dared not disobey your command. After asking why he had come, we picked two ginseng fruits and offered them to him. But that elder, with his worldly eyes and foolish heart, did not recognize the treasure of our immortal household. He said they were infants not yet three days old and repeatedly refused to eat them. So we disciples ate one apiece. Unexpectedly, among his three disciples was one surnamed Sun, named Wukong, who first stole four fruits and ate them. We disciples tried to reason with him and spoke a few words of plain truth. But he would not tolerate it and secretly employed a wondrous, unearthly art. How terrible! …” Reaching this point in their account, the two lads could no longer hold back the tears that streamed down their cheeks. The immortals asked, “Did that monk beat you?” Mingyue said, “He did not beat us. He only struck down our ginseng tree.” Hearing this, the Great Immortal showed no anger at all. He said, “Do not cry, do not cry. You do not know that the one surnamed Sun is himself an unfettered immortal of the Supreme Unity. He once caused havoc in Heaven and possesses immense magic powers. Since he has struck down the precious tree, would you recognize those monks if you saw them?” Qingfeng said, “We would recognize them all.” The Great Immortal said, “Since you recognize them, all of you follow me. —The rest of you disciples, prepare the instruments of punishment and wait until I return to beat them.” The immortals obeyed his command.

In alarm, Qingfeng bowed his head to the ground, while Mingyue kowtowed and said, “Master! Those monks from the east, whom you called your old friends, are a band of savage and ruthless robbers.”
The Great Immortal smiled. “Do not be frightened. Tell me slowly what happened.”
Qingfeng said, “Master, not long after you left that day, a Tang Monk from the Eastern Land did indeed arrive. There were four monks in his company, or five travelers counting the horse.
Your disciples dared not disobey your command. After asking why he had come, we picked two ginseng fruits and offered them to him.
But that elder, with his worldly eyes and foolish heart, did not recognize the treasure of our immortal household.
He said they were infants not yet three days old and repeatedly refused to eat them.
So we disciples ate one apiece.
Unexpectedly, among his three disciples was one surnamed Sun, named Wukong, who first stole four fruits and ate them.
We disciples tried to reason with him and spoke a few words of plain truth.
But he would not tolerate it and secretly employed a wondrous, unearthly art.
How terrible!
…” Reaching this point in their account, the two lads could no longer hold back the tears that streamed down their cheeks.
The immortals asked, “Did that monk beat you?”
Mingyue said, “He did not beat us. He only struck down our ginseng tree.”
Hearing this, the Great Immortal showed no anger at all. He said, “Do not cry, do not cry.
You do not know that the one surnamed Sun is himself an unfettered immortal of the Supreme Unity. He once caused havoc in Heaven and possesses immense magic powers.
Since he has struck down the precious tree, would you recognize those monks if you saw them?”
Qingfeng said, “We would recognize them all.”
The Great Immortal said, “Since you recognize them, all of you follow me.
—The rest of you disciples, prepare the instruments of punishment and wait until I return to beat them.”
The immortals obeyed his command.

p.src: The Great Immortal and his disciples Clear Breeze and Bright Moon mounted an auspicious cloud and set off in pursuit of Tripitaka, covering a thousand li in moments. From the clouds the Great Immortal looked westward, but saw no sign of the Tang monk. When he turned to look east, he found that he had overshot them by more than nine hundred li. It turned out that although the elder had ridden without stopping all night, he had covered only one hundred and twenty li; whereas a single surge of the Great Immortal's cloud had carried him over nine hundred li too far. One of the immortal boys said, “Master, that is the Tang monk sitting beneath the tree by the road.” The Great Immortal said, “I have seen him. You two go back and prepare the ropes. I shall capture him myself.” Clear Breeze and Bright Moon returned ahead of him, and we shall say no more of them for now.

p.src: He went straight to the tree and called aloud to the Tang monk, “Elder, this poor Daoist greets you.” The elder hurriedly returned the courtesy, saying, “Forgive me for not noticing you sooner.” The Great Immortal asked, “From where have you come, Elder? Why are you sitting in meditation here along the road?” Tripitaka replied, “This poor monk was sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. Passing this way, we have stopped here briefly to rest.” Feigning surprise, the Great Immortal said, “Since you have come from the east, did you happen to pass through my humble mountain?” The elder asked, “May I know which sacred mountain is yours, Immortal?” The Great Immortal replied, “The Wuzhuang Temple on Longevity Mountain is this poor Daoist's dwelling.”

p.src: At these words, Pilgrim, who had a guilty conscience, hastily answered, “No, no, we came by the main road.” The Great Immortal pointed at him and laughed. “You insolent monkey! Whom do you think you are deceiving? In my temple you knocked down my ginseng-fruit tree, then fled here during the night. Even now you refuse to confess—what are you trying to conceal? Do not try to escape. Return my tree at once!” Pilgrim grew furious at this. He drew his iron staff and, without another word, struck straight at the Great Immortal's head. The Great Immortal twisted aside, mounted an auspicious cloud, and rose directly into the air. Pilgrim also mounted a cloud and swiftly pursued him. p.src: With no regard for his opponent's rank or dignity, Pilgrim flailed wildly with his staff. The Great Immortal parried left and right with his jade fly whisk and endured his attack for two or three rounds. Then he employed the art called “The Universe in a Sleeve.” High in the clouds, he gently spread one robe sleeve into the wind; with a sudden sweep it came forward and enveloped all four monks together with the horse. Eight Rules cried, “This is bad! We have all been stuffed into a carrying sling!” Pilgrim said, “Idiot, this is no carrying sling. He has trapped us inside his sleeve.” Eight Rules said, “That is no great matter. Let me rake a hole through it so we can slip out. Then we shall simply say he was careless and failed to hold us securely, and that will be the end of it.” The idiot hacked about wildly with his rake, but it would not yield at all. Though it felt soft when pinched between the fingers, when struck it was harder than iron.

p.src: The Great Immortal turned his auspicious cloud about, descended straight into Wuzhuang Temple, seated himself, and ordered his disciples to bring ropes. The young immortals all stood ready to serve him. Watch as he plucked the Tang monk from his sleeve as though picking up a puppet, and bound him to a pillar beneath the eaves of the main hall. He took out the other three as well and tied each one to a separate pillar. He also took out the horse, tethered it in the courtyard, and gave it some fodder. The luggage was tossed beneath the gallery. Then he said, “Disciples, these monks are men who have left the secular life, so we must use neither blade nor spear nor subject them to axe or halberd. For now, bring me a leather whip and give them a beating, to vent the anger of my ginseng fruits.” The immortals hurriedly brought out a whip. It was made of no ordinary oxhide, sheepskin, deerskin, or calfskin, but was a Seven-Star Whip fashioned from dragon hide, which had been soaking in water. He ordered a strong young immortal to take hold of the whip. The boy asked, “Master, whom shall I beat first?” The Great Immortal replied, “Tang Tripitaka has shown the greatest disrespect. Beat him first.”

p.src: Hearing this, Pilgrim thought to himself, “My old monk cannot stand a beating. If they lash him until he is badly hurt, will that not be a sin of my making?” Unable to restrain himself, he spoke up. “Sir, you are mistaken. I stole the fruits, I ate the fruits, and I was the one who pushed down the tree. Why not beat me first? What purpose is there in beating him?” The Great Immortal laughed. “This insolent monkey speaks with surprising courage. In that case, beat him first.” The young immortal asked, “How many strokes?” The Great Immortal replied, “One for each fruit—thirty strokes.” The young immortal swung the whip and began to strike. Fearing the immortals' magic might be powerful, Pilgrim opened his eyes wide and watched closely to see where the blows would land. When he saw that the whip was aimed at his legs, Pilgrim twisted his waist and cried, “Change!” He transformed his legs into two bars of wrought iron, to see what the boy could do to them. The young immortal struck him thirty times, one blow after another, and by then it was nearly noon. The Great Immortal then commanded, “Tripitaka must also be beaten for failing to discipline his disciples and allowing this unruly follower to run wild.” The young immortal raised the whip again to strike. Pilgrim said, “Sir, you are mistaken again. When we stole the fruits, my master knew nothing of it. He was in the hall talking with your two boys; the deed was done by my brothers and me. Even if he is guilty of lax discipline, I, as his disciple, should take the beating for him. Beat me again.” The Great Immortal said, “Though this insolent monkey is crafty, treacherous, and unruly, he does possess some filial devotion. Since that is so, beat him again.” The young immortal gave him another thirty strokes. Pilgrim lowered his head and looked. His two legs were like bright mirrors, polished gleaming by the blows, yet he had felt neither pain nor itch. By then evening was approaching. The Great Immortal said, “Put the whip back in the water for now. We shall interrogate him under the lash again tomorrow morning.” The young immortals put the whip away to soak, and each returned to his room. After finishing their evening meal, they all retired to sleep, and we shall say no more of them.

p.src: Tears streaming from both eyes, the elder complained to his three disciples, “You caused this disaster, yet you have dragged me into suffering here with you. What are we to do?” Pilgrim said, “Stop complaining. Whenever there was a beating, I took it first. You have not suffered a single blow, so why are you moaning instead?” The Tang monk replied, “Though I have not been beaten, the ropes are hurting my body.” Friar Sand said, “Master, we are tied up here along with you.” Pilgrim said, “All of you, stop making a noise. In a little while we shall be on our way.” Eight Rules said, “Brother, you are bluffing again. These hemp ropes have been soaked with water and bind us fast. This is nothing like being locked in the hall, where you could use your lock-opening magic to force the door and escape.” Pilgrim replied, “This is no idle boast: let them soak even three-stranded hemp rope in water; even a palm-fiber hawser thick as a bowl would be no more to me than an autumn breeze.”

p.src: While they were speaking, all sounds had long since died away, and the heavenly thoroughfare lay still and deserted. The good Pilgrim shrank his body a little, slipped free of the ropes, and said, “Master, let us go.” Sha Monk cried in alarm, “Elder Brother, save us too!” “Quiet, quiet,” said Pilgrim. He untied Tripitaka, released Eight Rules and Sha Monk, straightened their short robes, saddled the horse, fetched the luggage from the corridor, and led them all out through the monastery gate. Then he told Eight Rules, “Go and cut down four willows by the cliff.” “What do you want them for?” asked Eight Rules. “They have a use,” said Pilgrim. “Fetch them quickly.” The fool possessed some brute strength. He went over and rooted up one tree with each thrust of his snout until he had four, then carried the whole armful back. Pilgrim broke off the treetops and told his two brothers to go back inside and bind them to the pillars with the original ropes, exactly as before. The Great Sage recited a spell, bit the tip of his tongue, spat blood upon the trees, and cried, “Change!” One became the elder, another became Pilgrim himself, and the remaining two became Sha Monk and Eight Rules. Each had precisely the same face and appearance as its original; it spoke when questioned and answered when called by name. Only then did the two brothers set off at a run and catch up with their master. All that night they pressed on without once reining in the horse, putting the Five Villages Abbey far behind them.

p.src: But at daybreak the elder began swaying in the saddle and nodding off. Seeing this, Pilgrim called, “Master, you cannot endure much! Why should a man who has left the world suffer so bitterly? I, Old Monkey, could go a thousand nights without sleep and never know the least weariness. Dismount for now, lest travelers see you and laugh. Rest awhile below the hillside, where we are sheltered from the wind and can recover our breath, and then we shall go on.”

p.src: We leave the master and disciples resting for a time beside the road. Instead, we tell how the Great Immortal rose at dawn, ate his morning meal, entered the hall, and ordered, “Bring the whip. Today it is Tang Tripitaka’s turn to be beaten.” The young immortal brandished the whip and said to the Tang monk, “I am going to beat you.” The willow answered, “Then beat me.” With resounding cracks, he struck it thirty times. He swung the whip toward Eight Rules and said, “I am going to beat you.” That willow too answered, “Then beat me.” When Sha Monk was beaten, his willow likewise answered that they should beat it. But when they came to beat Pilgrim, the real Pilgrim, far away on the road, suddenly shivered and cried, “This is bad!” “What do you mean?” asked Tripitaka. Pilgrim said, “I transformed four willows into the four of us, master and disciples. I thought that since they beat me twice yesterday, they would not beat me again today. But now they are striking my transformed double, and that is why my true body shivered. I had better withdraw the magic.” Pilgrim hurriedly recited a spell and recalled his magic.

At first we were beating the monk from the Great Tang, but now all we are striking are willow trunks.” Hearing this, the Great Immortal gave a cold chuckle and exclaimed in boundless admiration, “Sun Pilgrim truly is a fine Monkey King! If you fled, that might have been the end of it—but how dare you tie up some willows here to impersonate you? I shall never spare him. After them!”

p.src: The three brothers each raised his divine weapon and attacked together, while the Great Immortal parried them with nothing but his fly whisk. Before even half an hour had passed, he spread one sleeve of his robe and once again swept the four monks, the horse, and all their luggage into it at a stroke. Turning his cloud around, he returned to the abbey, where the immortals came to receive him. The immortal master seated himself in the hall and took his captives from his sleeve one by one. He had the Tang monk bound to a short pagoda tree below the steps, Eight Rules and Sha Monk each bound to a tree on either side, and Pilgrim tied up and thrown on the ground. Pilgrim said, “I suppose we are to be questioned.” In no time the binding was finished, and the Great Immortal ordered ten bolts of long cloth to be brought. Pilgrim laughed and said, “Eight Rules, this gentleman is most considerate. He has brought out cloth to make us lined jackets. Let us economize a little and make single-layer ones instead.” The young immortals carried out cloth woven on their household looms. The Great Immortal ordered, “Wrap Tang Tripitaka, Zhu Eight Rules, and Sha Monk in the cloth.” The immortals all came forward and wrapped them up. Pilgrim laughed and said, “Good, good, good! They are sewing the shrouds and laying you out already.” In a short while they had finished winding the cloth around them. Then the Great Immortal ordered them to bring out lacquer. The immortals promptly fetched raw and boiled lacquer they had gathered and dried themselves. They lacquered the cloth wrapped around the three men’s entire bodies, leaving only their heads and faces exposed. Eight Rules said, “Sir, the top does not matter much, but please leave an opening below so that we can relieve ourselves.” The Great Immortal next ordered them to carry out the great cauldron. Pilgrim laughed and said, “Eight Rules, what good fortune! They have brought out a cauldron—perhaps they mean to cook us a meal.” Eight Rules said, “That would be fine. Let us eat some rice; at least we shall die with full bellies and make respectable ghosts.” The immortals did indeed carry out a great cauldron and set it up below the steps. The Great Immortal ordered dry firewood piled beneath it and a fierce blaze kindled. “Fill the cauldron with clear oil. When it comes to a rolling boil, throw Sun Pilgrim in and fry him thoroughly, to avenge my ginseng-fruit tree.”

p.src: Hearing this, Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “That is exactly what Old Monkey would like. I have not bathed for some time, and my skin is rather dry and itchy. However it turns out, a good scalding will be most welcome. I am deeply obliged by their hospitality.” Before long, the oil in the cauldron was about to boil. Yet the Great Sage grew wary. Fearing that the immortal’s magic might be unfathomable and leave him unable to work a trick in the oil, he quickly looked around. East of the terrace stood a sundial platform, and to the west was a stone lion. Pilgrim gave a bound and rolled to the western side. He bit the tip of his tongue, spat a mouthful of blood upon the stone lion, and cried, “Change!” It changed into his exact likeness, bound into a bundle just as he was. His spirit then left his body, rose into the clouds, and looked down upon the Daoists.

p.src: A young immortal reported, “Master, the oil is boiling fiercely.” The Great Immortal ordered, “Carry Sun Pilgrim over and put him in.” Four immortal lads could not lift him. Eight could not lift him either, and even after four more joined them, he still would not budge. The immortals said, “This monkey is truly rooted to the soil. Small as he is, he is remarkably solid.” At last twenty young immortals hoisted him up and hurled him into the cauldron. There came a tremendous sizzle, and drops of boiling oil splashed up, scalding several large blisters onto the young Daoists’ faces. Then the fire-tending lad shouted, “The cauldron is leaking! The cauldron is leaking!” Before he had finished speaking, all the oil had drained away and the bottom of the cauldron had shattered. It turned out that a stone lion had been placed inside.

p.src: The Great Immortal flew into a rage. “That impudent ape is truly outrageous! He played his tricks right before our eyes. It would have been enough for you to flee, but why did you also smash my stove? There is no use trying to hold that wretched ape; even if we seize him, it is like shaping loose sand or grasping quicksilver, like clutching at shadows or catching the wind. Enough, enough, enough! Let him go. Untie Tang Sanzang instead, bring out a new cauldron, bind him up, and avenge the ginseng tree upon him.” The young immortals promptly set to work, undoing the cloth-and-lacquer bindings.

p.src: From midair, the Pilgrim heard every word clearly and thought, “Master could never withstand it. Once he is rolled in the oil, he will die; twice, and he will be scorched; after three or five rolls, they will have made him into a monk boiled to pulp. I had better go back and save him.” What a Great Sage! He lowered his cloud, stepped forward with hands respectfully folded, and said, “Do not ruin those cloth-and-lacquer bindings or bind my master. Wait for me to enter the oil cauldron instead.” The Great Immortal started in surprise and cursed, “You vile macaque! What trick did you use to smash my stove?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Whenever you encounter me, your stove is bound to fall. What has that to do with me? Just now I too wished to enjoy some of your affectionate hot oil, but my bowels and bladder were pressing. Had I relieved myself in the cauldron, I feared I might foul your cooked oil and make it unfit for seasoning your dishes. Now that I have thoroughly emptied myself, I am ready to enter the cauldron. Do not bind my master; come and bind me instead.” Hearing this, the Great Immortal gave a cold chuckle, strode out of the hall, and seized him in one grip.
